Howdy!

Does anyone have any suggestions on the best way to restrict a continuous MvPolynomial to {0,1}N\{0,1\}^N{0,1}N (i.e., N bit length strings)?

In particular, I am currently working with multivariate polynomials in [N][N][N] variables with coefficients in R\mathbb{R}R, and I am doing such a restriction by evaluating at functions of the form x:[N]→{0,1}x : [N] → \{0,1\}x:[N]→{0,1}. I need to be able to reason about the range of the resulting function (more info below).

However, my approach leads to some annoying proof states that make it unwieldy to work with and simplify. My code is below, if that's helpful at all.

Any suggestions would be great!

Thanks

Code:

import Mathlib

open MvPolynomial

noncomputable section

/- Define the first elementary symmetric polynomial in [N] variables. -/
def E₁N (N : Nat) : MvPolynomial (Fin N) ℝ := MvPolynomial.esymm (Fin N) ℝ 1

/- Takes a univariate constant to a multivariate constant. -/
def uniConstantBi (N : Nat) : ℝ →+* MvPolynomial (Fin N) ℝ where
  toFun := fun (x : ℝ) => C x
  map_one' := C_1
  map_mul' := fun x y ↦ C_mul
  map_zero' := C_0
  map_add' := fun x y ↦ C_add

/- Takes the polynomial q(t) into the polynomial q evaluated at x + y:
     q(t) ↦ q(x + y) -/
def substMapE₁N (N : Nat) (q : MvPolynomial (Fin 1) ℝ) : MvPolynomial (Fin N) ℝ :=
  MvPolynomial.eval₂Hom (f := uniConstantBi N) (fun (t : Fin 1) => E₁N N) q

/- Make a boolean bit value be interpreted as a real valued number. -/
def boolToReal (b : Bool) : ℝ :=
  if b then 1 else 0

example
    (N : Nat)
    (p : MvPolynomial (Fin N) ℝ)
    (h : IsSymmetric p) :
    -- ∃ q ∈ R[t]:
    ∃ q : MvPolynomial (Fin 1) ℝ,
      -- ∀ x ∈ {0,1}ᴺ : p(x₁, …, x_N) = q(x₁ + … + x_N)
      ∀ (x : Fin N → Bool),
        eval (fun i ↦ boolToReal (x i)) p =
          eval (fun i ↦ boolToReal (x i)) (substMapE₁N N q) := by

      apply Exists.intro

      /- Prove the witness is correct. -/
      case h =>
        intro x
        repeat' rw [MvPolynomial.eval_eq']
        -- (1) At this point, the proof state is very ugly.

      /- Witness -/
      case w =>
          sorry

h : p.IsSymmetric

  ∑ d ∈ (substMapE₁N N ?w).support, coeff d (substMapE₁N N ?w) * ∏ i, boolToReal (x i) ^ d i

Robin Arnez said:

Can you give an informal proof? Without an informal proof it's hard to understand what you're trying to do.

Yes of course! Apologies, its not always clear to me what level of detail is best when posting these kinds of questions.

Below I show a special case of $N=2$ (polynomials in 2 variables) and below that a sketch of the more general claim my lean code attempts to prove.

Claim 1: Let $p (x,y)$ be a real polynomial in $x$ and $y$ such that it is symmetric. Then there exists a real polynomial $q(t)$ such that $\forall x \in \{0,1\}^2: p (x, y) = q (x + y)$.

Proof: Let $p(x,y)$ be a symmetric polynomial. This means $p$ can be expanded in terms of the elementary symmetric polynomials.

In two variables, the elementary symmetric polynomials are $p_0 = 1$, $p_1 = x+y$ and $p_2 = xy$.
This means that

p(x,y)=c0+c1(x+y)+c2xy=c0+c1p1+c2p2p (x,y) = c_0 + c_1(x+y) + c_2 xy = c_0 + c_1p_1 + c_2 p_2p(x,y)=c0​+c1​(x+y)+c2​xy=c0​+c1​p1​+c2​p2​

For some constants $c_0, c_1, c_2$.

Observe,

p12=(x+y)2=x2+y2+2xy=p1+2p2p_1^2 = (x+y)^2 = x^2 + y^2 + 2xy = p_1 +2 p_2p12​=(x+y)2=x2+y2+2xy=p1​+2p2​
  ⟺  \iff⟺
p12=2p2+p1p_1^2 = 2p_2 + p_1p12​=2p2​+p1​
  ⟺  \iff⟺
p12−p1=2p2p_1^2 - p_1 = 2p_2p12​−p1​=2p2​
  ⟺  \iff⟺
p2=12p12−12p1p_2 = \frac{1}{2}p_1^2 - \frac{1}{2}p_1p2​=21​p12​−21​p1​

So

p(x,y)=c0+c1p1+c212p12−c212p1p (x,y) = c_0 + c_1p_1 + c_2 \frac{1}{2}p_1^2 - c_2\frac{1}{2}p_1p(x,y)=c0​+c1​p1​+c2​21​p12​−c2​21​p1​
  ⟺  \iff⟺
p(x,y)=c0+(c1−c212)p1+c212p12p (x,y) = c_0 + \left(c_1 - c_2\frac{1}{2}\right)p_1 + c_2 \frac{1}{2}p_1^2p(x,y)=c0​+(c1​−c2​21​)p1​+c2​21​p12​

Take

q(t)=c0+(c1−c212)t+c212t2q(t) = c_0 + \left(c_1 - c_2\frac{1}{2}\right)t + c_2 \frac{1}{2}t^2q(t)=c0​+(c1​−c2​21​)t+c2​21​t2

This gives the claim $\blacksquare$

More general claim and proof:

Claim 2: Let $p \in R[x_1,\dots, x_n]$ be a symmetric polynomial. We claim that there is a univariate polynomial $q\in R[t]$ such that

∀x∈{0,1}n ⁣:p(x1,…,xn)=q(x1+…+xn)\forall x\in \{0,1\}^n\colon \quad p(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = q(x_1 + \ldots + x_n)∀x∈{0,1}n:p(x1​,…,xn​)=q(x1​+…+xn​)

Proof:

Note that on $\{0,1\}^n$ we may assume $p$ is multilinear, since $x_i^k = x_i$ for all $k \geq 1$ there.

The Boolean restriction is what makes the reduction to $E_1$ possible: it bounds the number of elementary symmetric polynomials that can appear, and it is where the multilinearity assumption comes from.

Let $p \in R[x_1,\dots, x_n]$ be a symmetric polynomial. Then $p$ can be expressed as a linear combination of the elementary symmetric polynomial basis

p(x1,…,xn)=∑jdeg⁡(p)cjEj(x1,…,xn)p(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = \sum_j^{\deg(p)} c_jE_j(x_1, \ldots, x_n)p(x1​,…,xn​)=∑jdeg(p)​cj​Ej​(x1​,…,xn​)

where the $c_k$'s are constants and each $E_j$ is an elementary symmetric polynomial in $n$ variables. We will show that for each $E_j$ there is a univariate polynomial $q_j$ such that

∀x∈{0,1}n ⁣:Ej(x1,…,xn)=qj(x1+…+xn)andq(t)=∑k=1jdktk\forall x \in \{0,1\}^n\colon\quad E_j(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = q_j (x_1 + \ldots + x_n)\quad\text{and}\quad q (t) = \sum^{j}_{k=1} d_k t^k∀x∈{0,1}n:Ej​(x1​,…,xn​)=qj​(x1​+…+xn​)andq(t)=∑k=1j​dk​tk

We will use induction to show the claim. In particular, let $S(j)$ denote the following statement:

S(j) ⁣:Ej(x1,…,xn)=∑k=1jdkE1k(x1,…,xn)S(j)\colon E_j(x_1,\ldots, x_n) = \sum^{j}_{k=1} d_k E_1^k(x_1,\ldots, x_n)S(j):Ej​(x1​,…,xn​)=∑k=1j​dk​E1k​(x1​,…,xn​)

Base Case: $S(1)$

We need to show the following is true:

S(1) ⁣:E1(x1,…,xn)=∑k=11dkqk(x1+…+xn),   q∈R[t]S(1)\colon E_1(x_1,\ldots, x_n) = \sum^{1}_{k=1} d_k q_k \left(x_1 +\ldots + x_n\right), \space\space\space q \in R\left[t\right]S(1):E1​(x1​,…,xn​)=∑k=11​dk​qk​(x1​+…+xn​),   q∈R[t]

Trivially take $q(t) = t$; then $E_1 = q(E_1) = q \left(x_1 + \ldots + x_n\right)$.

This gives the claim.

Inductive Case: Suppose $S(j-1)$ is true for some $j\geq2$. That is, assume $E_{j-1}$ is a degree $j-1$ elementary polynomial such that

Ej−1(x1,…,xn)=∑k=1j−1dkE1k(x1,…,xn)E_{j-1}(x_1,\ldots, x_n) = \sum^{j-1}_{k=1} d_k E_1^k(x_1,\ldots, x_n)Ej−1​(x1​,…,xn​)=∑k=1j−1​dk​E1k​(x1​,…,xn​)

Then we want to show that $S(j)$ is true. That is, we want to show

Ej(x1,…,xn)=∑k=1jdkE1k(x1,…,xn)E_{j}(x_1,\ldots, x_n) = \sum^{j}_{k=1} d_k E_1^k(x_1,\ldots, x_n)Ej​(x1​,…,xn​)=∑k=1j​dk​E1k​(x1​,…,xn​)

Consider the product $E_1^j$. Note that the product of two symmetric polynomials is itself symmetric. Moreover, because of the Boolean restriction, every monomial in the expansion of $E_1^j$ reduces to one of exponent 1 in each variable. So we can write

E1j=∑kjdkEkE_1^j = \sum^j_k d_kE_kE1j​=∑kj​dk​Ek​

Split off the $j$th term:

E1j=djEj+∑kj−1dkEkE_1^j = d_jE_j + \sum^{j-1}_k d_kE_kE1j​=dj​Ej​+∑kj−1​dk​Ek​

Invoke the inductive hypothesis:

E1j=djEj+∑kj−1dkqk(E1)E_1^j = d_jE_j + \sum^{j-1}_k d_k q_k(E_1)E1j​=dj​Ej​+∑kj−1​dk​qk​(E1​)

Solve for $E_j$:

Ej=E1j+∑kj−1dkqk(E1)djE_j = \frac{E_1^j + \sum^{j-1}_k d_k q_k(E_1)}{d_j}Ej​=dj​E1j​+∑kj−1​dk​qk​(E1​)​

Ej=1dj[E1j+∑kj−1dkqk(E1)]E_j = \frac{1}{d_j}\left[E_1^j + \sum^{j-1}_k d_k q_k\left(E_1\right)\right]Ej​=dj​1​[E1j​+∑kj−1​dk​qk​(E1​)]

Take

qj(t)=1dj[tj+∑kj−1dkqk(t)]q_j(t) = \frac{1}{d_j}\left[t^j + \sum^{j-1}_k d_k q_k\left(t\right)\right]qj​(t)=dj​1​[tj+∑kj−1​dk​qk​(t)]

This gives the claim. $\blacksquare$
